question: to the Commission Marieke Ehlers (PfE), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Sebastian Kruis (PfE) Subject:

In the Commission’s latest attack on privacy, the President introduced an age verification app, describing it as ‘technically ready’ and built to ‘the highest privacy standards’. However, independent code reviews have revealed critical security flaws. The Commission is asked to answer the following questions: 1.

Researchers claim that the app’s PIN can be bypassed in under two minutes by editing a single local configuration file, thereby granting full access to another person’s credentials. Rate limiting and biometrics can reportedly be disabled in the same way. Is this accurate and how did this pass security reviews? If so, why should EU citizens continue to trust the Commission and its digital tools?

Does the app store unencrypted facial images from passport scans and selfies on the device without reliably deleting them? If so, how is this compatible with GDPR rules on biometric data, given that a private provider was recently fined nearly EUR 1 million in a similar case1?

The app’s repository describes it as ‘not feature-complete’ and requiring ‘further integration’. Why, then, did the Commission present it as technically ready, and will an independent security audit be required before any Member State deploys it?
https://www.dataguidance.com/news/spain-aepd-fines-yoti-eu950000-unlawful-processing.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The findings concern an early development version of the EU age verification (AV) software, that experts could examine and test before any use by citizens. The consortium released a hardening update on 17 April 20261 addressing the specific issues identified, and further updates will follow as the review process continues. The behaviours described require physical access to a device that has been modified to remove its built‑in security protections. On a standard, unmodified phone, the operating system itself prevents this kind of file access. The application (app) relies on local device processing and biometric material is used only to confirm that the user is the genuine holder of an authentic identity document, and it is never transmitted to anyone. The individual solutions published will need to comply with Regulation (EU) 2016/6792, which is supervised by the national data protection authorities. The Commission’s statement3 referred to the technical readiness of the publicly available EU AV blueprint. Further integration work must be performed by an app publisher, including translation, branding, app-store submission and operational hardening. The Commission Recommendation of 29 April 20264 explicitly calls on Member States to ensure compliance with all relevant cybersecurity standards. The EU AV Scheme will set out criteria for issuers of proof‑of‑age attestations and for AV solutions and will publish a list of providers that meet the required privacy and security standards.
